prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Before, The, Grating

outputs.L1:
Before balance, before counting, before the record glistens and the needle slides, grating, into the overture, there is the end of weight—the leaning into nothing, and then a caught breath. The record listens; the needle slides over slowly, and all at once, around us, a woman’s voice stretches weightless, leaning into nothing.

Like a clothesline, the taut chorus: oh, hilarious—oh baby. All around us, over slowly, a woman’s voice gathers above the “pick me up, pick me up” and the desperate “put, put me down.” First the tightrope, then the light foot, and the taunting chorus: “Pick me up, pick me up. Oh, oh baby.”

The slippery floor shimmers and spins like a record while the light swings footloose on its rope, out of time. The shadows slip, shimmering black, and spin across the floor, then turn back and pick up again.

Oh seedpod, caught for just one moment on the cattail, out of time, out of shadows; downy cheek against a beard: oh scratches on the record, oh baby, oh measure, oh strange balance that grips us on this side of the world.
outputs.L2:
Prior to equilibrium, prior to enumeration, before  
the disc flashes and the stylus drags, rasping,  
into the opening music, there comes the vanishing  
of heaviness—the tilt toward emptiness—and then  
a held inhale. The record seems to hear; the needle  
moves across it slowly, and suddenly, surrounding us,  
a woman’s singing unfurls, airy and unburdened,  
slanting toward nothing.

The chorus is stretched tight, like laundry cord:  
oh, laughing, oh darling—everywhere around us,  
gradually passing over, that woman’s voice  
rises above the plea, lift me, lift me,  
and the frantic answer, set me down, set me down.  
First comes the wire underfoot, then the delicate step,  
then the teasing refrain: lift me, lift me.  
Oh, oh darling.

The slick surface of the floor gleams and whirls  
as though it were a record, while the lamp swings freely  
from its cord, loose and out of rhythm.  
Dark shapes slide, glossy and black,  
spinning over the floorboards, then reverse  
and begin again.

Oh, seed case clinging for a single instant  
to the cattail; oh, suspended beyond time,  
beyond shade; soft cheek pressed against rough beard;  
oh, the record’s scuffs; oh darling; oh rhythm;  
oh, uncanny poise that holds us fast  
here on this half of the earth.
outputs.L3:
The poem evokes a moment that comes before balance, measurement, or counting, as if it begins in the brief pause before order takes shape. Sound enters the scene through the image of a record needle sliding into music, suggesting both delicacy and inevitability. This opening creates a sense of anticipation: the world of the poem is about to move, but it has not yet settled into rhythm or certainty.

At the center of this atmosphere is a woman’s voice, rising weightlessly through the scene. Her song seems to float above the physical world, surrounded by a repeated chorus of longing and release. The voice does not simply describe emotion; it becomes part of the movement of the poem itself. It lifts, circles, and returns, creating a feeling of desire that is both intimate and distant.

The poem’s imagery of tightropes, swinging light, and slippery floors reinforces this sense of instability. These images suggest a world in motion, where balance is difficult to maintain and every gesture carries risk. The tightrope implies danger and concentration, while the swinging light creates shifting shadows and uncertainty. The slippery floor adds to the feeling that nothing is fixed, and that the speaker or figures in the poem may lose their footing at any moment.

This instability is echoed in the repeated phrases “pick me up” and “put me down.” These words express a tension between wanting support and resisting control. To be picked up may suggest care, rescue, or desire, but it can also imply dependence or loss of agency. To be put down may suggest release, rejection, or the return to one’s own weight. The repetition of these phrases gives the poem a push-and-pull rhythm, capturing the complicated emotional space between attraction and resistance.

Through its connections between music, movement, shadow, and touch, the poem creates a strange and fragile sense of balance in an uncertain world. Nothing in the poem feels entirely stable, yet its sounds and images hold together through rhythm and repetition. The result is a poem that turns instability into a kind of music, suggesting that balance may not mean stillness, but the ability to move through uncertainty without completely falling.
outputs.L4:
The poem explores balance, weightlessness, music, and desire through a lyrical collage of images and repeated sounds. It moves between the physical and the dreamlike, using the record player as one of its central figures: a device that spins, repeats, lifts a needle, drops it again, and turns feeling into sound. This imagery gives the poem a circular motion, as though memory and desire are being played over and over like a song. The repeated fragments of music create a sense of longing, suggesting that human emotion is not always linear or stable, but rhythmic, recurring, and unfinished.

Throughout the poem, scenes shift quickly between motion, light, and touch. Bodies seem to rise, float, fall, and come into contact with the world around them. These movements create a feeling of suspension, as if the speaker is caught between gravity and release. The poem is interested in what it means to be held, carried, lifted, or set down, both physically and emotionally. Its language suggests that desire can make the body feel weightless, but also vulnerable. To be lifted is beautiful, but it also means trusting whatever holds you.

The record-player imagery deepens this idea of fragile balance. A record must spin evenly in order to make music; the needle must touch the surface with just enough pressure to produce sound without damaging it. This delicate relationship becomes a metaphor for embodied life. Human beings, like records, are marked by touch, repetition, and contact. Music emerges from friction, from the meeting of needle and groove, just as meaning emerges from the body’s encounters with the world.

The poem ultimately finds beauty in instability. It does not present balance as something fixed or easily achieved, but as something temporary and strange. Life is shown as a continual movement between being lifted and being put down, between pleasure and uncertainty, between the wish to escape the body and the need to inhabit it. In this way, the poem suggests that human experience is both graceful and precarious. Its music comes from that tension: the delicate, unstable balance of living in a body that can desire, move, fall, and be touched.
outputs.L5:
**Before The Grating**

Before the grating was placed across the old window, the room was filled with open light. Every morning, the sun slipped through the glass and painted thin golden lines across the floor. The house felt quiet but alive, as if it were waiting for someone to return.

The grating changed the way the light entered. Instead of pouring in freely, it arrived in patterns—small squares and narrow shadows. At first, it seemed harsh and unnecessary, a barrier between the room and the world outside. But over time, it became part of the room’s character.

Before, the window had offered only a view. The grating gave it texture, shape, and memory. It reminded anyone who looked through it that even barriers can create beauty, and even shadows can make the light more visible.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical free-verse poem inspired by a vinyl record playing an old jazz song, weaving in themes of balance, weightlessness, dancing, and repeated fragments like “pick me up” and “put me down.”
counterfactuals.output:
The needle lowers—  
a small moon finding its orbit  
in the black lake of the record.  

Then crackle,  
then brass,  
then a piano walking barefoot  
through a room full of blue smoke.  

Pick me up,  
the trumpet says,  
bright as a match in the dark.  

Put me down,  
answers the bass,  
all velvet and gravity,  
all thumbprint and root.  

And the old song turns,  
turns,  
turns—  
a slow plate of night  
balanced on one silver point.  

I am light enough to drift,  
heavy enough to stay.  
One foot on the floorboard,  
one foot in the air,  
I learn the secret math  
of dancing:  

how the body can be an anchor  
and a balloon,  
a question  
and its answer,  
a glass filled to the brim  
with falling stars.  

Pick me up—  
the saxophone bends its gold back  
toward heaven.  

Put me down—  
the drum brushes whisper  
over the skin of the earth.  

Somewhere,  
a singer who has been gone for years  
leans close to the microphone  
and breathes my name  
as if it were smoke,  
as if it were mercy,  
as if it were the last blue note  
held between two hands.  

The record spins its black weather.  
The room sways.  
The lamp becomes a ballroom moon.  
Dust rises in tiny couples,  
all of them weightless,  
all of them keeping time.  

Pick me up,  
put me down,  
pick me up,  
put me down—  

the heart knows this rhythm.  
The heel and the wing.  
The lift and the landing.  
The ache and the yes.  

I turn with the song  
until I am less body  
than balance,  
less hunger  
than hum,  

until even sorrow  
wears polished shoes  
and asks me, gently,  
for one more dance.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a poem in the style of a contemporary ekphrastic meditation on a record needle dropping, a woman’s voice singing, and a couple dancing on a slippery floor, with surreal imagery and recurring phrases.
counterfactuals.output:
**Needle / Voice / Floor**

Look: the needle lowers  
like a black bird choosing water.

Before the song, there is the small weather  
of dust, the room holding its breath  
in a blue glass lung.

Then—  
a woman’s voice opens  
from the groove,

not arriving, exactly,  
but being unburied.

She sings as if the moon  
has been folded into her throat.  
She sings as if every window  
once had a body leaning from it.

Look: the needle lowers.  
Look: the floor begins to remember rain.

The couple step out  
onto the polished dark,  
onto the varnish slick as a frozen lake,  
onto the ballroom of spilled stars.

His hand at her back  
is a question in a white glove.  
Her hand in his  
is a door refusing to close.

They turn, and the room turns with them—  
lamps loosening their halos,  
chairs growing antlers,  
the wallpaper breathing roses  
into the mouths of the mirrors.

The woman sings,  
and her voice is a staircase made of smoke.  
The woman sings,  
and the smoke climbs itself.

Look: the needle lowers  
again and again,  
though it has already fallen.

Isn’t this how longing works—  
a circle pretending to travel,  
a wound with a velvet edge,  
a name you keep placing  
on the tongue of the machine?

The couple glide,  
then almost fall.  
Their shoes whisper warnings  
in the language of ice.

The floor is slippery.  
The floor is a river.  
The floor is the back  
of a sleeping animal dreaming  
it is a river.

Still they dance.

Around them, the record spins  
its black planet,  
its one bright scratch  
like lightning trapped under skin.

Her voice pours out—  
honey, ash, a match struck underwater.  
Her voice wears a red dress  
no one can touch.

And the couple, shining with danger,  
lean into each turn  
as if falling were merely  
another form of listening.

Look: the needle lowers.  
Look: the floor begins to remember rain.  
Look: their bodies make a shelter  
and call it music.

When the song cracks,  
a flock of silver fish  
leaps from the speaker.  
When the chorus returns,  
the ceiling opens  
its slow mechanical flowers.

The woman sings  
what cannot be held.  
The couple hold each other.

This is the painting inside the sound:  
black circle, silver thorn,  
a mouth of fire,  
two figures skating  
across the beautiful catastrophe  
of shine.

And when the record ends,  
it does not end.

The needle stays  
in its tiny ruined orbit.

The woman’s voice  
keeps walking through the walls.

The couple, still turning,  
still slipping,  
still almost saved,

dance on the floor  
that remembers rain,

dance on the floor  
that remembers rain,

dance on the floor  
that remembers rain.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a dense, musical free verse poem that begins “Before balance, before counting” and includes images of a glistening record, a sliding needle, a taut chorus, shadows spinning, and the line “Oh strange balance that grips us.”
counterfactuals.output:
Before balance, before counting  
there was the glistening record, black moon  
turning its weather beneath a sliding needle,  
a silver insect tasting the storm.

The room leaned inward.  
Walls held their breath in plastered octaves.  
Shadows spinning from our shoulders  
became dancers, became dials, became the dark  
multiplying itself into rhythm.

We were not yet numbers,  
not yet names pinned to the pulse,  
only bodies caught in the taut chorus  
of what wanted to rise  
and what had to remain.

Oh strange balance that grips us.  
One foot in hunger, one in hymn,  
one hand full of ash, the other  
lifting a cup of bright noise to the mouth.

Listen—  
even silence has a spine,  
even sorrow sways when the bass begins,  
and the heart, that old turntable,  
keeps dragging its bright needle  
through the groove of us,

finding music  
where the wound repeats.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: I need an experimental poem about sound, gravity, and intimacy: a phonograph record starts, a female voice fills the room, the lyrics “pick me up, put me down” echo, and the scene becomes a meditation on balance and being held.
counterfactuals.output:
The record lowers its black weather  
onto the room.

Needle: a small moon  
falling correctly.

Then static—  
the furniture remembers rain,  
the walls lean in,  
even the dust arranges itself  
around the first note.

A woman’s voice enters  
not through the door  
but through the floorboards,  
through the glass of water,  
through the soft hinge  
between breath and listening.

She sings:

*pick me up, put me down*  
*pick me up, put me down*

and the words become a pendulum,  
a cradle,  
a law of motion with a pulse.

I stand there  
with my hands open  
as if balance were something  
that could be caught  
without being possessed.

Gravity is not only falling.  
Sometimes it is the mercy  
of being answered by a surface.  
The bed holding the body.  
The body holding a name.  
The name held in the mouth  
until it warms.

*pick me up, put me down*

The record turns  
like a planet practicing tenderness.  
Its groove is a wound  
that knows how to repeat itself  
without disappearing.

I think of all the ways  
we ask to be carried:

lift me from the bathwater  
of my own thinking,

set me back  
where I can feel the ground,

do not keep me in the air  
as proof of your strength,

do not drop me  
as proof of my weight.

The voice keeps circling.  
It does not rescue.  
It steadies.

Sound is touch  
without hands.

The room fills with her singing  
until the ceiling grows deeper,  
until my ribs become a bowl  
and something invisible  
is placed there carefully.

*pick me up, put me down*

Love, maybe, is this:

not flight,  
not ownership,

but the practiced art  
of pressure and release,

the knowing  
when to gather,

when to let the beloved  
meet the earth again.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a modernist-style poem with no stanza breaks that uses repetition, enjambment, and sensory imagery around an old record, a swinging light, a tightrope, a seedpod on a cattail, and lovers caught between lifting and falling.
counterfactuals.output:
The old record turns, turns, under the needle’s small weather,  
a black moon clicking its scratches into rain, into rain,  
and the room tastes of dust, warm shellac, orange peel,  
the swinging light cuts us in pieces, returns us, cuts us,  
your face arriving then leaving in the yellow arc,  
my hand half-raised, half-ashamed of wanting to be held,  
above us the wire of the tightrope hums like a nerve,  
like a streetcar cable in winter, like a song we cannot keep,  
and we are on it, aren’t we, we are always on it,  
lovers with our shoes full of sky, our mouths full of floor,  
between lifting and falling, lifting and falling,  
the record says yes, the record says no, the record says yes  
in its cracked circular tongue, and outside by the ditch  
a cattail leans with its brown seedpod loosening,  
soft ruin, velvet fuse, a thousand small departures  
waiting for one hard breath, one hand, one weather,  
to open it into flight, into fluff, into nothing that touches  
everything, and the light swings, swings, the needle worries  
the groove, the wire shines thin as a cut in the dark,  
you lean toward me as if gravity were a rumor,  
I lean away as if flight were a debt, and still  
our shadows meet on the wall before we do, rise before we rise,  
fall before we fall, and the old record turns, turns,  
its music smelling of rain on iron, of wool coats, of lips  
after crying, and the cattail breaks somewhere in the mind,  
spilling its pale seeds over the ditch, over the wire,  
over the room where we balance, where we tremble,  
where we are lifted by what drops us, dropped  
by what lifts us, the light swinging, the song repeating,  
the floor waiting with its dark, patient hands.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
